title: Dual Fuel HVAC | This Old House
summary: This Old House adds a cold-climate inverter heat pump coil to an existing 92% furnace to make a dual-fuel system in an 1894 house.

assertions.quote: We found this 92% furnace here, and instead of throwing it away, we said it's got plenty of life left.

verdicts.note: Mass Save offers partial-home rebates to customers who keep an existing boiler or furnace to supplement a new heat pump; the page shows this is a recognized setup but does not measure the fuel savings.

Integrating a ducted ccASHP with the existing furnace proved complicated: it needed a same-brand communicating furnace and a multi-stage fan, which most 80% and older condensing furnaces lack, so the project installed new furnaces.
Mini-splits added alongside existing heating cut the baseline fuel by about 3.8-4.7 MMBtu per unit in winter 2016 on average, at a cost of about 763 kWh of electricity.
Gas backup may be the most attractive option for households whose gas furnace does not yet need replacing, but the fuel saving from adding a heat pump is not quantified.

assertions.quote: homeowner can decide based on the cost of fuel whether they want to go with gas or heat pump.

verdicts.note: Hybrid heat pumps with fossil backup are said to mitigate bill increases without necessarily raising upfront cost, but they were not analysed.
The authors note private economics might improve if supplemental heat came from gas rather than resistance, but they do not model it.

Switching between heat pump and fuel at the crossover temperature is cheapest in principle, but at 2016 prices the gas crossover was above 70 F for the measured units, so pairing with gas saved nothing; only a modelled HSPF-13 unit (28-40 F crossover) would beat gas alone.

Lifetime-cost model: in Toronto a heat pump with gas backup is cheapest for nearly all households, and in Edmonton for 1940 and 1980 detached and townhouses, but gas with AC wins other Edmonton cases; this is lifetime cost including equipment, not running cost alone.

assertions.quote: And what will this heat down to? Al: Negative 22.

verdicts.note: RMI's modelled cold-climate unit provides substantial heat down to -13F (COP 1.4 there), based on manufacturer performance data.

A ductless cold-climate unit delivered a consistent median capacity from 10F to -15F and kept operating to -25F at reduced capacity, though the authors say it needs backup below -15F; one monitored unit.
Among these ducted variable-speed units, Site 10's compressor did not run below 0F despite a disabled lockout, and the dual-fuel unit did not run below about 4F.

Even non-cold-climate mini-splits from 2012-14 kept operating below 0 F (at lower efficiency than cold-climate models), with COPs averaging about 1.5 at -10 to 0 F; capacity at those temperatures was not measured directly.

The prototype cold-climate units ran mainly in heat-pump-only mode even in the lowest outdoor bins, with resistance-only operation minimal above 0 F; but only 8 of 22 sites logged 10+ hours below 0 F, and auxiliary heat was on about 25% of the time at -10 to 0 F.
Cold-climate heat pumps can perform well down to -25°C (about -13°F), citing NRCan, though backup may still be needed in the coldest parts of Canada.

assertions.quote: what it's trying to do is to find heat even in the cold air outside

verdicts.note: Electricity does the work of moving heat rather than producing it, so delivered heat per unit of electricity is typically much greater than one.
RMI states that because heat pumps move heat rather than generate it they are more efficient than electric furnaces and baseboard heat; its modelled heat pumps run at COPs above 1.

The paper explains that ASHPs transfer rather than generate heat and so output more heat energy than the electricity they use; its measured annual COPs (1.9 all-electric, heat-pump-only COPs up to about 3.5) confirm output above input.

Metered mini-splits in Massachusetts and Rhode Island averaged a COP of about 1.5 even at -10 to 0 F, so they delivered more heat than the electricity they used even in the coldest bins (rated COPs are higher).

In 22 field homes, prototype cold-climate heat pumps had median heat-pump-only COPs of 1.6-2.7 below 30 F and 1.9 at 0-5 F, so they delivered roughly two units of heat per unit of electricity even in deep cold.

UK quasi-experiment on 1,321 Octopus Energy heat pump adopters: gas use fell 9,351 kWh/yr while electricity rose 3,080 kWh/yr, so the heat pump replaced gas using only about 30% of the energy, in line with roughly 300% efficiency.
Heat pumps move heat rather than generating it and deliver 2 to 5 kWh of heat per kWh of electricity (citing NRCan and others).

assertions.quote: In a cold climate like this, we've got to make sure it's above the snow line

verdicts.note: Manufacturers require raised mounting in snowy climates so snow does not block airflow and defrost water can drain.

Field staff found many outdoor units mounted with too little clearance, where roof melt and defrost water could freeze and impair the fan, and the manufacturer's guidance implies about four inches; this supports raised mounting but gives no 'snow line' rule.
